To use “y” to replace a place: j’y vais, j’y habite.
To use “en” for a quantity: j’en ai trois, j’en veux.

To put y / en in the right place, including in the past and with an infinitive.
To talk about moving house: boxes, furniture, carrying.
Saturday, 5 April. Ioana and Julien are moving into the new flat. Karim and Radu (who came all the way from Romania!) are helping them. There’s a lot of work.
Right, the van has arrived. How many boxes are there?
I counted forty-two. And half of them are my books!
Forty-two! Are there many left in your old flat?
No, there’s nothing left. Everything’s in the van. Except Victor, who’s already in the new flat!
How did he get in there? The door was locked!
Through the courtyard window. He went there all by himself this morning.
Radu, can you help me with the sofa? It’s very heavy.
Sure. We take it up to the first floor? Let’s go!
Careful, there’s a wardrobe too. Do you have a screwdriver?
Yes, I have one in the toolbox. It’s in the kitchen.
(Two hours later) Break! Who wants coffee? I made a big flask.
I’d love some! And did Sophie bring us croissants?
Yes, she brought about a dozen. But Radu has already eaten four…
Five! Carrying furniture makes you hungry. And the piano, when is it coming?
On Monday. Professional movers will bring it. I’m not touching it, it’s too fragile!
Right, ten more boxes and we’re done. Come on, back to work!

“J’y vais” = “zhee vay”. “Il y va” = “ee-lee va”. Y attaches itself to the word before.
“J’en ai” = “zhã-nay”, with a liaison on n. “Il en a” = “ee-lã-na”.
It’s said very fast: “ee-nya-na-plü”. Learn it as one block.
Douzaine = “doo-zen”, a dozen (12). Likewise: une dizaine (about 10), une vingtaine (about 20), une centaine (about 100).
Dé-mé-na-ger: four equal syllables, stress on the last one. With a closed é, as in “say” without the glide.
“Y” replaces a place introduced by à, en, dans, chez, sur… English says “there” or nothing at all: “Are you going to Lyon? — Yes, I am.” In French, “y” is required.
Are you going to Lyon? — Yes, I am (going there).
Do you live in France? — Yes, I’ve lived there since September.
Is Victor in the flat? — Yes, he is (there).
You can’t just say “Oui, je vais.” The verb “aller” needs a destination, so you add “y”: “Oui, j’y vais.” Likewise “On y va !” (Let’s go!).
“Y” also replaces “à + a thing” after verbs like penser à, réfléchir à, toucher à: “Tu penses à ton examen ? — Oui, j’y pense.” (I’m thinking about it.)
“En” replaces a noun preceded by a partitive (du, de la, des) or by a number / quantity. English sometimes uses “some” or “of them”: “I have two (of them)”, “I want some”.
Il y a beaucoup de livres ?
Oui, il y en a beaucoup.
Non, il n’y en a plus.
With a number or quantity, the number STAYS at the end: “J’en ai deux” (I have two), “J’en veux un peu” (I want a little). Only the noun disappears.
“En” also replaces “de + a place” (= from there): “Tu viens de Paris ? — Oui, j’en viens.” (Yes, I’ve come from there.)
The choice depends on the article: a specific object (definite article) → le, la, les. A quantity (partitive, number, des) → en.
Are you taking the sofa (that one)? → Yes, I’m taking it.
Are you having croissants? → Yes, I am.
Have you got the key? → Yes, I’ve got it.
Have you got a key? → Yes, I’ve got one.
Same rules as for the other pronouns: before the verb, the auxiliary or the infinitive.
Je n’y vais pas. / Je n’en ai pas.
J’y suis allée. / J’en ai mangé quatre.
Je vais y aller. / Je veux en acheter.
In the imperative, -er verbs get their -s back before y and en, for pronunciation: “Va !” but “Vas-y !” (Go on!), “Mange !” but “Manges-en !”.
Very common fixed expressions: “Vas-y !” (Go on! Go for it!), “Allez-y !” (Go ahead! After you!), “On y va !” (Let’s go!), “Je m’en vais” (I’m leaving).
to move out / to move in
to carry the furniture up / down

On Monday morning at eight o’clock, the whole of rue d’Austerlitz was at the window. The piano was arriving.
The movers looked at the staircase. It was narrow and it turned a lot. “Up the stairs? Impossible. You can’t get through there.”
So they called a crane. It arrived an hour later, yellow and enormous, and it blocked the whole street.
Julien was very nervous. He couldn’t watch. Ioana, on the other hand, was taking photos. She took at least fifty.
Sophie came out of her bakery with a tray of croissants. “Would you like some? They’re for the show!” The movers took two each.
Madame Bernard came too, with Victor in her arms. “I once saw a piano fly, in 1975, in Marseille. It fell.” Julien went white as a sheet.
But this piano didn’t fall. It rose slowly, went through the window and came into the living room. Everyone applauded.
In the evening the boxes were still everywhere. There were some in the kitchen, in the bedroom, and even in the bathroom.
But Julien only had eyes for the piano. He sat down, opened the lid… and found an old yellow envelope inside.
In the envelope there was a handwritten score. At the top someone had written: “For Hélène, for her twentieth birthday. Lyon, 1962.”
“Who’s Hélène?” asked Ioana. “I’ve no idea,” said Julien. “The seller didn’t say anything about it.”
So he put the score on the piano and began to play. It was a waltz, gentle and a little sad.
Ioana sat down on a box and listened. Outside, the street was quiet. Victor was already on the piano, as if he had always lived there.
When the music stopped, Ioana said: “Tomorrow I’ll call the seller. I want to know who Hélène was.” Julien smiled. He wanted to know too.
